title: Canus at the board
hook: condemned by Caligula, Julius Canus finished his board game calmly (On Tranquility 14)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was remissio: Socrates on the floor with the children, and the mind rising sharper after rest. Your line was put the seriousness down.

Rome, around the year 40. A man named Julius Canus has just finished a long argument with the emperor Caligula. As he turns to leave, Caligula tells him not to get his hopes up: he's already ordered his execution. Canus says: thank you, most excellent prince. Seneca admits he isn't sure what Canus meant. Was it irony, showing how cruel Caligula was if death came as a relief? Or real thanks? Either way, the next ten days are why On Tranquility remembers him.
screen: `CALIGULA: I'VE ORDERED YOUR DEATH.` → `THANK YOU, MOST EXCELLENT PRINCE.` → `TEN DAYS LEFT.`

segments.voice: First, the ten days. Roman custom then gave a condemned man ten days before execution. Canus spent them, Seneca says, without any sign of anxiety. Not hiding, not pleading, not bargaining. Living. Second, the board. When the centurion came, Canus was in the middle of a board game, a Roman strategy game played with little soldier pieces. He didn't jump up. He counted the pieces and told his opponent: don't go claiming after I'm dead that you won. Then he nodded to the centurion: you're my witness, I'm one piece ahead. Do you think Canus was only playing a game at that board, Seneca asks? He was making a mockery of the tyrant. Third, the last question. His friends were weeping, and Canus asked why they were sad. You're always arguing about whether the soul lives on, he said; I'm about to find out. He meant to watch closely, in that last moment, to see whether the mind could feel itself leaving, and if he learned anything he'd come back and tell them. The sources are silent on what happened next. Fourth, what we take from it. Not that death is nothing, or that we should be cheerful facing cruelty. Canus was under a tyrant's sentence, and the story is a loss as well as an example. What stays is the board. Under the worst pressure there is, he finished what was in front of him, honestly, and kept score fairly. An ordinary deadline can borrow that.
screen: `TEN DAYS WITHOUT ANXIETY.` · `I'M ONE PIECE AHEAD.` · `I'M ABOUT TO FIND OUT.` · `FINISH WHAT'S IN FRONT OF YOU.` · then, large: `FINISH THE GAME.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're in the middle of that pressure keeps tempting you to rush or abandon. Picture the pressure arriving like a knock at the door, and picture yourself not jumping up: you look at the board, count what's done and what's left, and make the next fair move. Calm isn't the absence of the knock; it's finishing the move.
Latrunculi. Latin for little soldiers, the board game Canus was playing when the centurion came: he counted the pieces and finished the game. Today's word.
Your line: finish the game. Pressure knocks, and the next fair move is still yours. That's day five hundred two.

howItsDone: Readers of Seneca often remember Julius Canus when under pressure, finishing the task at hand calmly and fairly before reacting.

chat.says: Why does Seneca admire a man who kept playing a game before his execution?
options: He stayed calm, finished what was in front of him, and kept score honestly.
He'd secretly been pardoned, so he knew the soldiers wouldn't harm him.
He hoped Caligula would be impressed by his game and cancel the order.
chat.meaning: Seneca admires Canus' calm: ten days without anxiety, and at the end he counted the pieces and finished the game, mocking the tyrant.

notes: On Tranquility 14.4–10 paraphrased: Canus' long dispute with Caligula; 'gratias ago, optime princeps'; Seneca's uncertainty about the meaning; ten days without anxiety; the board game (ludus latrunculorum), counting the pieces, 'you'll be witness I'm one ahead'; the friends' grief; his plan to observe whether the soul perceives its departure and report back. Confirm.
Date 'around the year 40' and the ten-day rule (senatus consultum of AD 21 under Tiberius; Tacitus Annals 3.51) are commonly cited; confirm.
The philosopher accompanying Canus ('philosophus suus'): confirm.
